terms.title: Key terms
terms.blurb: Define it and say why it matters.

cards.def: The older belief that diseases like cholera spread through bad air from rotting matter.
cards.sig: Wrong about the cause, but it still drove sewer and sanitation reforms that saved lives.

cards.def: The idea that specific microorganisms cause specific diseases, established by Pasteur and Koch in the 1860s to 1880s.
cards.sig: Shifted public health from clearing bad air to finding and stopping specific pathogens.

cards.def: The nineteenth-century push in Britain, led by reformers like Edwin Chadwick, for clean water, sewers, and better housing.
cards.sig: Made government responsible for the conditions that cause disease.

cards.def: Separating people who may have been exposed to a disease. The word comes from the 40 days ships waited offshore in plague-era Venice.
cards.sig: One of the oldest public health tools, and still a debate about liberty versus protection.

cards.def: When enough of a population is immune that a disease cannot spread easily, which protects people who are not immune.
cards.sig: Explains why vaccination is a community decision, not only a personal one.

cards.def: The global campaign that ended smallpox, declared eradicated by the World Health Organization in 1980.
cards.sig: The only human disease eradicated so far: proof that coordinated global action can work.

cards.def: The study of how disease is distributed in populations, and what drives it.
cards.sig: Turns individual cases into patterns that can guide action.

cards.def: The conditions where people are born, live, work, and age that shape their health.
cards.sig: Moves attention from individual behavior to housing, income, and policy.

sources.title: Primary sources
sources.blurb: The 5 W's, the context, and the significance.

cards.name: John Snow's cholera map
cards.what: A map of cholera deaths clustered around the Broad Street water pump.
cards.why: To show that cholera spread through water, not air.
cards.context: Miasma theory dominated, and germ theory was not yet accepted.
cards.significance: A founding example of epidemiology: data on a map changed a local decision, and the pump handle was removed.
cards.use: Argue that evidence can overturn an accepted theory, even before anyone knows the mechanism.

cards.name: Jenner's Inquiry on cowpox
cards.who: Edward Jenner, an English country doctor.
cards.what: His report that cowpox infection protected people against smallpox.
cards.why: To share the results of inoculating people with cowpox.
cards.context: Smallpox killed and scarred millions, and the older method, variolation, was risky.
cards.significance: The start of vaccination; the word vaccine comes from vacca, Latin for cow.
cards.use: Argue that a cheap intervention can change history, and discuss the ethics of testing it on a child.

cards.name: The Black Report
cards.who: A UK working group chaired by Sir Douglas Black.
cards.what: A report showing large health gaps between social classes in Britain.
cards.why: Commissioned to explain inequalities that persisted despite universal care.
cards.context: The National Health Service had provided care free at the point of use since 1948.
cards.significance: Showed that free care alone does not close health gaps; living conditions matter.
cards.use: Argue that access to care is not the same as equal health.

nameThat.title: Name that source
nameThat.blurb: Identify a source from a short description.

cards.text: A map of deaths around a single water pump in London.
cards.clue: A water pump plus clustered deaths: evidence against bad air.

cards.text: A country doctor reports that people who caught cowpox did not get smallpox.
cards.clue: Cowpox points to the first vaccine.

cards.text: A government report finds the poorest workers die years earlier, even with free health care.
cards.clue: Free care, yet gaps by social class remain.

cards.def: Governments protecting health through laws, funding, and enforcement.
cards.ask: Who gained power when the state took responsibility for health, and who lost freedom?

cards.def: Experts whose evidence changed what societies believed about disease.
examples: Koch's identification of the cholera bacterium
cards.ask: How did new evidence win, or lose, against accepted beliefs?

essays.title: Essay builder
essays.blurb: Build an essay one step at a time.
checklist: The thesis answers the prompt and makes an argument.
Three examples, each from a different period or place.
One primary source discussed in detail, not just named.
Every paragraph ties back to the thesis.
The conclusion says why the argument matters.

prompts.q: Was public health progress driven more by science or by politics? Use at least three examples.
prompts.thesis: Science supplied the tools, but politics decided when, and for whom, public health advanced.
bodies: Victorian sewers were built on miasma theory, which was wrong science, because politics made clean cities a priority.
Smallpox had a vaccine from 1798, but only global cooperation in the 1960s and 1970s finished the job.
Source paragraph: Snow's 1854 cholera map. Evidence persuaded local officials to remove one pump handle, while the belief in bad air took decades to fade.
prompts.conclusion: Science makes progress possible; political choices decide whether it happens.

prompts.q: Does access to health care explain differences in health? Argue with three examples.
prompts.thesis: Access matters, but living conditions explain more of the gap than care does.
bodies: Cholera deaths fell with clean water before any cure existed.
Smallpox fell where vaccination reached everyone, which shows prevention works best when it is universal.
Source paragraph: the Black Report (1980) found class gaps in death rates in Britain despite free care since 1948.
prompts.conclusion: Closing health gaps takes housing, income, and clean environments, not only clinics.
